scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The dance originated from the Alur people's process of mixing and smearing mud on their houses.
Over time, these utilitarian movements were refined into a formal dance.
It became a royal tradition performed for the Rwot (King) and was historically used in rituals to appease gods for rain or successful harvests.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Agwara is performed for royal celebrations, clan competitions, and thanksgiving for good harvests.
It also has historical roots in lunar festivals and rituals for rain or agricultural success.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Dancers perform in linear and circular formations.
The technique involves specific twisting of the legs and waist.
Both men and women participate, often wearing ankle bells to provide a percussive accompaniment to their footwork.
Watch for Mud-smearing twist.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The dance is named after the 'agwara' horns, which are long trumpets.
These are accompanied by drums.
Listen for the Agwara horns (long trumpets), Drums, Ankle bells.
The sound is dominated by the resonant, heraldic tones of long wooden trumpets (agwara) and the steady pulse of drums, punctuated by the sharp, metallic jingling of dancers' ankle bells.

scenes.title: The people
narration: The Rwot (King of the Alur) is the central figure for whom the royal versions of the dance are performed.
There are three primary variants: 'Kwaya' and 'Mbaka', which are competitive and royal forms lasting two days, and 'Selewa', which is a shorter form used for general thanksgiving.
The dance is a traditional heritage of the Alur people of Northern Uganda and the West Nile sub-region.

scenes.title: Step A — slowly
